goals: Explain why companies hold stock and what it costs.
Set minimum, maximum and reorder point levels.
Calculate safety stock, including when lead time varies.
Calculate the economic order quantity (EOQ) and its total cost.
Use ABC analysis to decide how closely to control each item.
Keep stock records accurate with FIFO/FEFO, cycle counting and stock turnover.

handout.intro: Stock is a buffer between supply and demand. Too much ties up cash and space; too little loses sales. This session gives you the tools to hold the right amount, and to prove it with numbers.

sections.h: 1. Why hold stock, and what it costs

blocks.p: Stock protects against **demand spikes, supplier delays and production problems**. Think of it as insurance: it protects you, but it has a premium.

head: Type of cost
What it includes
rows: Cash tied up, warehouse space, insurance, damage, theft, expiry and obsolescence
Admin work, transport and receiving for each order
Lost sales, unhappy customers, stopped production lines

blocks.p: Types of stock: **raw materials**, **work in progress**, **finished goods** and **MRO** (maintenance, repair and operating supplies, such as spare parts).

list: **Minimum (buffer)** – the stock you always want to keep, to cover delays or spikes.
**Maximum** – the most worth holding; above this, space and cash are wasted.
**Reorder point (ROP)** – when stock falls to this level, order again.

callout.title: Reorder point formula
callout.text: **ROP = (average daily demand × lead time in days) + safety stock**. Example: 80 units a day × 7 days + 200 safety stock = **760 units**. When stock reaches 760, order. If demand is normal, about 200 units will be left when the new stock arrives.

blocks.p: Safety stock covers the **variation** around average demand and lead time. Choose a **service level** and its Z value: 90% → 1.28, 95% → 1.65, 99% → 2.33.

head: When
Formula
Example
rows: Demand and lead time both vary
SS = (max demand × max lead time) − (average demand × average lead time)

blocks.p: σd = standard deviation of demand per period; LT = lead time in the same periods; σLT = standard deviation of lead time.

callout.title: The point
callout.text: When a supplier’s lead time is unreliable, safety stock almost doubles in the example above. Making the supplier reliable can cut stock and cash.

sections.h: 4. How much to order: the EOQ

blocks.p: Ordering often costs more in ordering costs; ordering a lot costs more in holding costs. The **economic order quantity** balances the two.

callout.title: EOQ formula
callout.text: **EOQ = √(2 × D × S ÷ H)**. D = annual demand, S = cost per order, H = holding cost per unit per year.

blocks.p: Use the ROP and EOQ together: the **reorder point says when**, the **EOQ says how much**. Adjust for pack sizes, supplier discounts, space and shelf life.
Sort items by **yearly value** (units × cost). Usually a small number of items make most of the value (the 80/20 idea).

head: Class
Typical share
Control
Count
rows: About 20% of items, about 80% of value
About 30% of items, about 15% of value
About 50% of items, about 5% of value
Simple rules, more stock is fine

blocks.p: Value is not everything: a cheap item can still be **critical** (for example, a medicine or a spare part that stops a machine).

list: **FIFO** – first in, first out: oldest stock is used first.
**FEFO** – first expired, first out: the item that expires soonest goes first. Essential for food and medicines.
**LIFO** (last in, first out) is rarely right for physical stock, and is **not allowed for accounting under IFRS** (IAS 2), which Qatar uses.

blocks.p: **Cycle counting** – count a small part of the stock regularly (A items monthly, B quarterly, C once or twice a year) instead of one big count a year. When the count and the system differ, **find the cause** (receiving errors, wrong location, theft) – do not just correct the number.
Aim for inventory record accuracy of **99% or better**.

sections.h: 7. Inventory turnover and days of stock

callout.title: Formulas
callout.text: **Average stock** = (opening + closing) ÷ 2. **Turnover** = cost of goods sold ÷ average stock. **Days of stock** = 365 ÷ turnover.

blocks.p: Example: cost of goods sold 1,200,000; opening stock 180,000; closing stock 220,000. Average = 200,000. Turnover = **6 times a year**. Days of stock = 365 ÷ 6 = **61 days**.
Higher turnover usually means less cash tied up. Compare with your own history and your industry.

head: Problem
Common causes
What to do
rows: Demand fell but levels were not changed; big discount orders; optimistic forecasts
Find slow movers early; return, discount or write off; lower the maximum
Demand spike; supplier delay; safety stock too low; wrong records
Recalculate safety stock; improve supplier reliability; fix records

blocks.p: Review levels **monthly** for important items. A level that was right six months ago may be wrong today.

terms.meaning: The cost of keeping stock: cash, space, insurance, damage, expiry.
Running out of an item when customers want it.
terms.example: Hospitals wait five days for a medicine.

terms.meaning: The stock level that triggers a new order.
Time from placing an order to receiving it.
Extra stock that covers variation in demand and lead time.
The chance that safety stock covers demand during the lead time.
Economic order quantity: the order size with the lowest total ordering and holding cost.
Sorting items by yearly value into A, B and C classes.
First in, first out: use the oldest stock first.
terms.example: Pick from the pallet that arrived first.

terms.meaning: First expired, first out: use the stock that expires soonest first.
terms.example: Yoghurt with the nearest expiry date is sent first.

terms.meaning: Counting a small part of stock regularly instead of all at once.
How many times stock is sold and replaced in a year.
How many days the average stock would last.
Stock losing value because it is out of date or no longer wanted.
terms.example: Old phone covers after a new model launch.

quiz.q: Daily demand 50, lead time 6 days, safety stock 100. What is the reorder point?
D = 8,000 per year, S = 50 per order, H = 2 per unit per year. What is the EOQ?
Which Z value matches a 95% service level?
A supplier’s lead time becomes less reliable. What happens to the safety stock you need?
quiz.why: More variation in lead time means more uncertainty, so more safety stock is needed.

quiz.q: At the EOQ, how do yearly ordering cost and yearly holding cost compare?
quiz.why: The EOQ is exactly where the two costs balance.

quiz.q: In ABC analysis, which items get the tightest control?
quiz.why: A items are a small number of items with most of the value, so they deserve the most attention.

quiz.q: A pharmacy warehouse should usually pick medicines using…
quiz.why: First expired, first out avoids medicines expiring on the shelf.

quiz.q: Cost of goods sold 900,000; average stock 150,000. What is the inventory turnover?
A cycle count finds 20 fewer units than the system shows. What should you do first?
options: Change the system number and move on
Investigate the cause (receiving, picking, location, theft)
quiz.why: Fix the process, not just the number, or the error will come back.

quiz.q: Demand for an item fell from 200 to 60 a month, but nobody changed its reorder point. What is the likely result?
quiz.why: Old, high levels keep ordering too much for the new, lower demand.

workbook.intro: Use the EOQ, Reorder point, Safety stock, ABC analysis and Turnover tools to check your answers.

questions.prompt: A Doha pharmacy chain sells 120 boxes of a medicine per day. The supplier takes 5 days. Safety stock is 240 boxes. Calculate the reorder point and explain what it means for the stock controller.
questions.hint: ROP = demand × lead time + safety stock.

questions.prompt: Weekly demand averages 400 units with a standard deviation of 60. Lead time is 3 weeks. Calculate safety stock for 95% service (Z = 1.65). Show your working.
Annual demand is 20,000 units, each order costs 100 and holding costs 4 per unit per year. Calculate the EOQ, the number of orders per year and the total yearly cost.
questions.hint: Check that ordering cost and holding cost are equal.

questions.prompt: Choose five items a supermarket in Qatar stocks. Estimate yearly units and cost, and put them into A, B and C classes. Explain one exception where a C item still needs close control.
A cycle count shows the system is wrong for 8% of locations. Give three possible causes and one fix for each.
Why is FEFO better than FIFO for yoghurt?

How confident are you with today's topic?
